text: By default, Data Factory Studio authors directly against the live service — every change either gets published immediately, or it genuinely doesn't exist at all. That means no draft state for half-finished work, no real collaboration model with code review, and no ARM template for the factory itself. Connecting a real Git repository fixes all three at once.

Every Git-connected factory has a collaboration branch, main by default — the only branch you can actually publish from. Real work happens on feature branches instead: create one, make your changes, and save freely, with no publish validation required until you're genuinely ready.

When you're ready to bring those changes into the shared branch, you open a real pull request right from the branch dropdown — routing you straight into Azure Repos or GitHub's own review flow, with comments and approval, exactly like reviewing application code.

Here's the constraint that makes the whole model genuinely coherent: Publish is only available when you're on the collaboration branch. You cannot publish directly from a feature branch, by design — which is exactly what makes can-edit-can't-publish from Lesson 49 work in practice.

Publishing doesn't touch the collaboration branch directly — it generates ARM templates representing your published factory state and writes them to a separate branch, adf_publish by default. That's what your CI slash CD release pipeline actually deploys from. The collaboration branch is never a live reflection of what's running — it has to be published, manually or through automation, to take effect.

One deliberate exception worth remembering: Data Factory never writes secrets into Git. A linked service still using a raw password publishes immediately the moment you save it, bypassing the Git workflow entirely for that one resource — precisely why the Key Vault pattern from Lesson 48 matters here specifically. Next: Publishing and Environments — taking that ARM template from dev to test to production.
